In a 3D printer that deposits material in layers on top of each other, what sort of file format is used to store the shape of the item on a computer? Is it succeeding layers of STL?
What file format does a 3D printer use?

I think the .STL format is the defacto standard. I know shapeways and a bunch of other 3D printer companies accept it. I am not sure what you mean by succeeding layers of STL. Say you want to 3D print Master Chief from Halo. You would pose him as you want, make sure he is one model, not a bunch of separate models like his helmet being separate from torso. You select that model and export it as a .STL.

If you want to make sure it's printable I'd recommend creating a Shapeways account and uploading it there. By default your models are private and they have a bunch of tools to check thickness and such if your software doesn't have any.
Used to work for Stratasys Manufacturing. Can confirm. .STL is the way to go.

What you do is model whatever you want to print in whatever modeling program you want. Then find a way to export to .stl, this is what your "Slicer" reads. Your slicer is a program that slices the files into instructions that your printer reads (called G-Code), and you finally feed the G code to your printer to print.

If you want help with anything related to 3D printing I'm happy to help, just shoot me a PM or reply here and I'll do what I can.

The 3D printer understands gcode, that is basically a compiled model into movement and temperature instructions.

In regard to the model, it depends on what your slicer software understands. It has to import that model and convert it to gcode. You cannot directly import a 3D model to print because the model has no clue what printer you are going to use, used plastic support material. It must be compiled to gcode first.

STL files are used the most I think.
